211.title: Cut down the forest (280–289)
211.hook: cut down the whole forest of desire, not just one tree; death sweeps off the distracted like a flood a sleeping village
211.howItsDone: Teachers in many Buddhist traditions quote the forest verse when explaining that practice aims at craving itself, not only at its separate outlets; monks and lay students often memorize the Pali line.

segments.voice: Yesterday, all created things, and your line: all things pass. What three changing things did you watch? Day two hundred eleven, and the last day of chapter twenty, the way.

You decide to quit one thing. Say it's the late-night snack. You keep the promise for a week, and you feel strong. Then you notice you're scrolling until one in the morning instead. Or buying things you don't need. The snack was gone, but whatever wanted the snack just found another door. Anyone who has tried to change a habit knows this game of whack-a-mole. Today's verses name it with a picture that has made readers smile for two thousand years, because it's also a pun. Today: cut down the forest.
screen: `QUIT ONE THING.` → `IT COMES BACK SOMEWHERE ELSE.` → `A PICTURE, AND A PUN.`

segments.voice: Verses two hundred eighty to two hundred eighty-nine close the chapter on the way. They open with a warning about the young and strong who never get around to rousing themselves: the path doesn't walk itself. Then verse two hundred eighty-three, which says, in plain words: cut down the whole forest of desire, not just one tree. Here's the pun. In Pali, the word vana means a forest, and vana also means desire, longing. So the Buddha is saying: cut down the vana, the forest and the wanting both. Not one tree. You can chop down the snack tree, and the forest simply grows another one next to it. The verse goes on: when you've cleared both the forest and the undergrowth, you are free of the woods. The next verses show how deep the roots go. As long as desire is not cut, the mind stays tied, the text says, like a calf that won't leave its mother's side. Then comes the sharpest picture in the chapter. A man, proud of his children and his herds, with his mind on everything else, is carried off by death the way a flood carries off a sleeping village. In the night, while everyone dreams. The verses aren't trying to frighten. They're saying that time is the one thing desire keeps us from noticing. Sons and fathers and relatives can't shelter anyone from it, the text goes on, and so the wise person, seeing this, clears the road now. Buddhist teachers read this as practical advice. Cutting one tree is still worth doing. But the aim is to look past the tree to the forest, the wanting underneath, and to start while the village is still awake.
screen: `ROUSE YOURSELF: THE PATH WON'T WALK ITSELF.` · `VANA — FOREST, AND DESIRE.` · `THE FLOOD AND THE SLEEPING VILLAGE.` · `CLEAR THE ROAD NOW.` · then, large: `CUT THE FOREST.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Think of one small desire that came up today. A snack, a purchase, a check of the phone. Just one tree. Now, gently, look behind it. What was the wanting underneath? Boredom, maybe, or tiredness, or wanting to feel a little better. Don't fight it. Just see the forest behind the tree, and name it quietly to yourself. Then let the naming go and come back to the breath, in and out. The bell holds the time.
Cut down the forest. In Pali, vana is both a forest and a desire: cut the whole wanting, not one tree.
Your line: cut the forest. Today, trim one desire, just one, and when it tries to pop up somewhere else, smile at the forest. Day two hundred eleven.

212.title: The bigger joy (290–295)
212.hook: if by leaving a small pleasure one finds a great one, the wise leave the small
212.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use verse 290 to explain renunciation not as loss but as trading a lesser happiness for a greater one; the riddle verses 294–295 are usually taught with the commentary's symbolic reading.

segments.voice: Yesterday, cut down the forest, and your line: cut the forest. Did the desire you trimmed pop up somewhere else? Day two hundred twelve, and chapter twenty-one begins.
screen: `CUT DOWN THE FOREST — CUT THE FOREST.`

segments.voice: There's a famous experiment with children and marshmallows. One now, or two if you can wait. Most of us know how that feels from the inside: the phone at dinner, when you'd really rather talk to the person across the table. The extra hour in bed, when you'd rather have the quiet morning walk. It isn't that the small pleasure is evil. It's that it sits right in front of the bigger one, blocking the view. A chapter the translator simply called miscellaneous opens with exactly this trade. Today: the bigger joy.
screen: `ONE MARSHMALLOW NOW, OR TWO?` → `THE SMALL PLEASURE BLOCKS THE VIEW.` → `A CHAPTER CALLED MISCELLANEOUS.`

segments.voice: Chapter twenty-one is a gathering of verses that didn't fit elsewhere, and it starts with one of the clearest in the book. Verse two hundred ninety, in Max Müller's English: "If by leaving a small pleasure one sees a great pleasure, let a wise man leave the small pleasure, and look to the great." Notice the verse doesn't say pleasure is bad. The Pali word is sukha, which means happiness, ease, sweetness. The verse wants more of it, not less. It's a trade, and the wise person makes the good one. The next verse tells you what a bad trade looks like: the one who seeks happiness for himself by causing pain to others gets tangled up in hatred and never gets free. Then the verses turn to attention. People neglect what ought to be done and do what ought not, the text says, and their troubles grow; but those who keep watch over the body, moment by moment, don't drift that way. Then comes the strangest pair of verses in the whole book, two hundred ninety-four and two hundred ninety-five. They say the true brahmana goes free, even after killing mother and father and two kings. Read on its own, it's shocking. The old commentary explains it as a riddle. The mother is craving, the father is pride, the kings are two wrong views, and the kingdom is the senses and everything that rides on them. Kill those, and you walk free. It's the forest from yesterday, told as a riddle. The bigger joy, in the end, is the freedom on the far side of all the small trades.
screen: `SUKHA — HAPPINESS, EASE, SWEETNESS.` · `A BAD TRADE: JOY BUILT ON PAIN.` · `KEEP WATCH OVER THE BODY.` · `THE RIDDLE OF MOTHER, FATHER, KINGS.` · then, large: `THE BIGGER JOY.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Bring to mind one small pleasure you reach for most days. Nothing dramatic: a snack, a scroll, a few more minutes in bed. Now ask, quietly, what bigger joy it sometimes stands in front of. A conversation, a rested morning, a clear head. You don't have to give anything up yet. Just see the two side by side, the small and the great. Then let both go, and rest in the breath, which asks nothing of you. The bell holds the time.
The bigger joy. Leave a small pleasure when it hides a great one: the verse wants more happiness, not less.
Your line: the bigger joy. Today, trade one small pleasure for the bigger one it was hiding, and notice how the trade feels afterward. Day two hundred twelve.

213.title: Well awake (296–305)
213.hook: the disciples of Gotama are always well awake, day and night their minds on the Buddha, the dhamma, the sangha
213.howItsDone: Many Buddhists recall the Buddha, the dhamma and the sangha at the start and end of the day, often with a bow and a short Pali homage before a home shrine; Theravada teachers call this recollection of the three jewels.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bigger joy, and your line was the same: the bigger joy. Which small pleasure did you trade, and for what? Day two hundred thirteen.

What's the last thing on your mind before you fall asleep? For a lot of us it's the glow of a screen, a worry about tomorrow, or a replay of something awkward we said at lunch. And the first thing in the morning is usually the same worry, picking up where it left off. Whatever the mind rests on at the edges of the day tends to color everything in between. Today's verses describe people whose minds rest somewhere else, day and night, and they use the word that gives the Buddha his name. Today: well awake.
screen: `THE LAST THING BEFORE SLEEP.` → `THE FIRST THING IN THE MORNING.` → `WHERE THE MIND RESTS.`

segments.voice: Verse two hundred ninety-six, in Max Müller's English: "The disciples of Gotama (Buddha) are always well awake, and their thoughts day and night are always set on Buddha." Gotama is the Buddha's family name. And the words for well awake come from the same root as the word Buddha itself, budh, to wake up. A buddha is one who has woken. His students, the verse says, are well awake too. Then the verse repeats, like a chant, six times over. Well awake, their thoughts set on the Buddha. Then on the dhamma, the teaching. Then on the sangha, the community. Müller, writing in 1881, translated sangha as the church, which tells you something about his own world. Those first three are the three jewels from camp three, the three things Buddhists go to for refuge. The next three verses keep going: their thoughts set on the body, then delighting in harmlessness, then delighting in meditation. So well awake doesn't mean never sleeping. It means that the mind has a home to return to. The rest of the chapter gathers other sayings. Leaving the world is hard, the text says, and living in a household is hard too, and both have their pains. Good people shine from far away like the Himalayas, while the bad go unseen, like arrows shot at night. And the chapter ends with a picture of the one who sits alone, sleeps alone, walks alone, and finds joy in it, as if living in a forest. In many Buddhist homes, the three jewels are recalled at the end of the day, before sleep: a short homage, a bow, a moment of remembering.
screen: `BUDH — TO WAKE UP.` · `BUDDHA, DHAMMA, SANGHA, DAY AND NIGHT.` · `A HOME FOR THE MIND.` · `SHINING LIKE THE HIMALAYAS.` · then, large: `WELL AWAKE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and let the body settle as if it were bedtime. Now let three things pass slowly through your mind, one with each breath. The Buddha: someone who woke up. The dhamma: the teaching, and the way things are. The sangha: all the people, past and present, who have walked this path. If you're simply learning, just hold the three names, the way you'd hold three stones in your hand. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Well awake. From budh, to wake, the same root as Buddha: a mind that keeps returning home, day and night.
Your line: well awake. Tonight, before you sleep, let the three jewels be the last thing on your mind, even for three breaths. Day two hundred thirteen.

214.title: Grasp it rightly (306–311)
214.hook: the liar goes downward; kusa grass grasped wrongly cuts the hand
214.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers use the kusa-grass verse to warn that practice held with pride or harshness does harm; kusa grass itself was long used in India for mats and ritual, and the tradition says the Buddha sat on a bundle of it on the night of his awakening.

segments.voice: Yesterday, well awake, and your line was the same: well awake. Were the three jewels the last thing on your mind last night? Day two hundred fourteen, and chapter twenty-two, the downward course.

If you've ever pulled a blade of tall grass through your fingers the wrong way, you know it can slice you like paper. The grass didn't change. The way you held it did. Pick it up by the base and pull it straight, and it comes away clean. Grab it along the edge, and it bites. In India there's a grass called kusa, sharp-edged, used for centuries in ritual and for sitting mats. Today's verses use it to say something about how we hold even good things. Today: grasp it rightly.
screen: `A BLADE OF GRASS CAN CUT.` → `KUSA — SHARP-EDGED, SACRED.` → `HOW YOU HOLD IT.`

segments.voice: Chapter twenty-two is called the downward course, and it's the chapter where the Dhammapada speaks most bluntly about what happens after harm. It opens with lying. The one who says what didn't happen goes downward, the text says, and so does the one who did something and says, I didn't do it. In Buddhist teaching, the downward course means rebirth in painful states, and Müller translates it as hell; but in Buddhist teaching these states don't last forever: they end when the karma that caused them runs out. The next verses aim at monks who wear the yellow robe but live badly. Better to swallow a red-hot iron ball, one verse says, than to eat the village's offered food while living that way. Then verse three hundred eleven, in Max Müller's English: "As a grass-blade, if badly grasped, cuts the arm, badly-practised asceticism leads to hell." Here's the surprise. The warning isn't about bad things. It's about good ones, held wrongly. The monk's life, the practice, the discipline, can cut you if you grab it by the edge. Held with pride, it becomes a way to feel superior. Held with harshness, it becomes self-punishment. Held with show, it becomes a costume. The next verses say the same about half-hearted practice: a loose, careless effort only scatters more dust. For anyone learning a path, including this one, it's a useful mirror. A daily sit, a precept, a kind act can each be held rightly: lightly, honestly, by the base. Or they can be held by the edge. The grass is the same either way.
screen: `THE DOWNWARD COURSE BEGINS WITH A LIE.` · `THE ROBE WITHOUT THE LIFE.` · `GOOD THINGS, GRASPED BADLY, CUT.` · `HOLD IT BY THE BASE.` · then, large: `GRASP IT RIGHT.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Rest your hands open on your lap. Think of one good thing you do regularly: a habit, a practice, a way you help someone. Ask, gently, how you're holding it. By the base, lightly and honestly? Or by the edge, with a little pride, or a little harshness toward yourself? No verdict needed. Just notice the grip. Then let your hands stay open, and let the breath come and go on its own. The bell holds the time.
Grasp it rightly. Kusa grass, held by the edge, cuts the hand: even a good practice, held badly, can hurt.
Your line: grasp it right. Today, handle one thing carefully, a cup, a conversation, a task, and notice what changes when you hold it by the base. Day two hundred fourteen.

215.title: The frontier fort (312–319)
215.hook: guard yourself like a border town, guarded within and without
215.howItsDone: Buddhist monastics and lay practitioners train in guarding the sense doors, noticing what comes in through the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind; teachers often use the frontier-fort verse to describe it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, grasp it rightly, and your line: grasp it right. What did you handle carefully, and did it feel different? Day two hundred fifteen, the second day of the downward course.

Think of an old town on a frontier. Not a capital, with its big armies, but a small place at the edge, where trouble arrives first. The people there can't afford to be casual. They know which gate is weak, which stretch of wall is crumbling, which night the guards get sleepy. They check them all, every day, and inside the walls they keep order too. In the time of the Buddha, kingdoms kept towns like this along their borders. Today's verse asks you to be one. Today: the frontier fort.
screen: `A TOWN AT THE EDGE.` → `TROUBLE ARRIVES FIRST.` → `THE WEAK GATE, THE SLEEPY GUARD.`

segments.voice: The chapter on the downward course keeps going with a run of plain advice. A slack effort, a vow half kept, a doubtful discipline: none of these brings much fruit. If something is worth doing, do it with your whole strength. A bad deed is better left undone, one verse says, because it burns you afterward; a good deed is better done, because it doesn't. Then comes verse three hundred fifteen, in Max Müller's English: "Like a well-guarded frontier fort, with defences within and without, so let a man guard himself." Within and without. The walls face outward, against what comes in through the senses: the ad, the insult, the easy temptation. But the fort also keeps watch inside, over the moods and thoughts that start their own trouble. The verse goes on: don't let a moment slip past, because those who miss their moment grieve later. The last verses of the chapter are a surprise. They're about shame and fear aimed at the wrong target. Some people are ashamed of what isn't shameful, and not ashamed of what is. Some fear what isn't dangerous, and shrug at what is. They see wrong where there is none and miss it where it is. So guarding the fort isn't the same as being anxious about everything. A good guard knows which gate is actually weak. Buddhist teaching has a word for this guarding: restraint of the senses, keeping watch at the doors of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind. It isn't a wall to hide behind. It's attention, placed where it's needed.
screen: `DO IT WITH YOUR WHOLE STRENGTH.` · `A FORT GUARDED WITHIN AND WITHOUT.` · `SHAME AND FEAR AT THE WRONG TARGET.` · `KNOW WHICH GATE IS WEAK.` · then, large: `GUARD THE BORDER TOWN.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Walk the walls of your own town for a moment. Where does trouble usually get in for you? Maybe a gate on the outside: a certain app, a certain conversation, a certain time of night. Or a gate on the inside: a mood that turns sour, a thought that loops. Pick just one weak spot. Picture a calm guard standing there, not angry, just awake. Then rest in the breath. The bell holds the time.
The frontier fort. A border town guarded within and without: watch the gates of the senses, and the mind inside.
Your line: guard the border town. Today, guard the one weak spot you found, just for today, and notice how often trouble comes knocking at that gate. Day two hundred fifteen.

216.title: Bearing the arrow (320–324)
216.hook: as the elephant in battle bears the arrow, I will bear harsh words
216.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers pair verse 320 with the commentary's story of Magandiya's hired insults; khanti, patience, is trained as a daily practice and counted among the perfections in both Theravada and Mahayana teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the frontier fort, and your line: guard the border town. Which gate did you guard, and how often did trouble knock? Day two hundred sixteen, and chapter twenty-three, the elephant.
screen: `THE FRONTIER FORT — GUARD THE BORDER TOWN.`

segments.voice: Someone says something harsh about you. Maybe online, maybe across a table, maybe behind your back and it comes around. Your body reacts before you do: face hot, heart fast, a reply already typing itself in your head. And a small voice says: let's just leave. Change the group chat, change the job, change the town. The old commentary on today's verse tells of a morning when the Buddha's companion said almost exactly that. Today: bearing the arrow.
screen: `SOMEONE SAYS SOMETHING HARSH.` → `THE REPLY TYPES ITSELF.` → `LET'S JUST LEAVE.`

segments.voice: Verse three hundred twenty, in Max Müller's English: "Silently shall I endure abuse as the elephant in battle endures the arrow sent from the bow: for the world is ill-natured." The commentary's story goes like this. In the city of Kosambi, a woman named Magandiya held a grudge against the Buddha, and she paid people to follow him and his monks through the streets, shouting insults. Ananda, the Buddha's attendant, had had enough. Let's go to another town, he said. The Buddha asked: and if they abuse us there? Then another town, said Ananda. The Buddha said a problem should be settled where it arises, and he spoke this verse. The abuse, the story says, faded within a week. The picture is a war elephant. In ancient India, elephants were trained to walk into battle and take arrows without turning to trample their own side. The next verses say a tamed elephant is the one the king rides, and the best among people is the one who has tamed himself and can bear hard words. Mules, fine horses and great elephants are all good when trained, but the one who trains himself is better still. And no animal, however fine, can carry you to the untrodden place; only a tamed self goes there. Bearing isn't pretending it didn't hurt. The arrow still lands. The elephant just doesn't stampede. In Buddhist teaching this is khanti, patience or forbearance, one of the qualities a person on the path trains, again and again, one arrow at a time.
screen: `MAGANDIYA'S HIRED INSULTS.` · `ANANDA: LET'S LEAVE TOWN.` · `THE WAR ELEPHANT DOESN'T STAMPEDE.` · `KHANTI — PATIENCE THAT BEARS.` · then, large: `BEAR THE ARROW.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, feet on the ground, heavy like an elephant. Bring back one small criticism you've received lately. Keep it small. Let the words land, and notice where they land in the body: the chest, the jaw, the belly. Don't argue with them. Don't agree either. Just stand, the way the elephant stands, feeling the sting and not turning to trample. Breathe into that spot. Then let the criticism go, and rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Bearing the arrow. Like a war elephant that takes the arrow and doesn't stampede: patience with harsh words.
Your line: bear the arrow. Today, when one criticism comes your way, take one breath before you answer, and let the elephant stand. Day two hundred sixteen.

217.title: Alone in the forest (325–333)
217.hook: if you find no good companion, walk alone like an elephant in the forest
217.howItsDone: Buddhist tradition values both good spiritual friendship and time in solitude; monks go on solitary retreats, and the Parileyya elephant who served the Buddha appears in temple art across South and Southeast Asia.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bearing the arrow, and your line: bear the arrow. Did a criticism come, and did the elephant stand? Day two hundred seventeen, the end of the week and of the elephant chapter.

A lot of people are afraid of being alone. A table for one, a weekend with no plans, a quiet apartment: it can feel like proof that something's wrong. So we fill the silence with company, even company that leaves us worse off. Today's verses have a different picture. A great elephant, walking by itself through the forest, unhurried, needing nothing from the herd. The commentary says the Buddha himself once spent a rainy season like that, in a forest, with an elephant for a companion. Today: alone in the forest.
screen: `A TABLE FOR ONE.` → `COMPANY THAT LEAVES YOU WORSE.` → `AN ELEPHANT, UNHURRIED.`

segments.voice: The elephant chapter ends with a run of verses about the mind and about company. First the mind: it used to wander wherever it pleased, one verse says, but now I will hold it, the way a trainer with a hook holds an elephant in rut. Pull yourself out of the bad road like an elephant pulling itself out of the mud. Then company. If you find a wise, good friend to walk with, the text says, walk with them gladly. If you don't, walk alone. Verse three hundred thirty, in Max Müller's English: "It is better to live alone, there is no companionship with a fool; let a man walk alone, let him commit no sin, with few wishes, like an elephant in the forest." The commentary sets these verses after a bitter quarrel among the monks of Kosambi, the same city as yesterday's story. The monks wouldn't make peace, so the Buddha left and spent a rains retreat in the Parileyya forest, where, the story says, a great elephant who had also left his noisy herd looked after him. Notice what the verse doesn't say. It doesn't say people are bad or that friendship is a trap. Earlier chapters praised good company over and over, and the next verse says friends are sweet when need comes. It says: good company first, and if that's missing, your own company, kept clean and simple, beats bad company. Alone, not lonely. This week you cut the forest, traded for the bigger joy, stayed well awake, grasped it rightly, guarded the border town and bore the arrow. The elephant closes the week walking by itself, content.

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. For this sit, you are the elephant in the forest. No one needs anything from you, and you need nothing from anyone. Notice how that feels: a little strange, maybe, or a relief. Listen to whatever sounds are near, the way an elephant listens to the trees. If loneliness shows up, let it sit beside you like another animal in the clearing. You don't have to send it away. Then rest in the breath, alone and content. The bell holds the time.
Alone in the forest. With no good companion, walk alone, with few wishes, like an elephant in the forest.
Your line: alone, not lonely. Today, give yourself one hour alone, a walk, a meal, a quiet room, and enjoy your own company on purpose. Day two hundred seventeen.

original.note: Pali ekacara: one who walks alone; verse 330 uses the verb 'eko care' (let one walk alone).

trapdoor: what you thought: 'alone in the forest' means cutting yourself off from people.
what it means: good company first; if there's none, your own company, simple and clean, beats bad company.
what a scholar hears: the same image, 'eko care', echoes the Rhinoceros Sutta of the Sutta Nipata (Sn 1.3), and the Parileyya story is told in the Vinaya and the commentaries.
